frontmatter.title: Paying a Multimodal Model to Find Rectangles
frontmatter.summary: A detection pipeline nobody can see has three defects that compound — and the expensive one is not the one to fix first.
frontmatter.coverAlt: Comic panel regions across a dark field — most drawn at near-invisible opacity, three rendered in lit rose with polygon vertices, cut by gutter-profile scan lines.
frontmatter.authorNote: Written while fixing my own pipeline, including the bug in it that told me a confident lie.

seo.title: Paying a Multimodal Model to Find Rectangles
seo.description: 1,162 detections nobody has ever seen. Write-only inference, shared-egress rate limits, and why observability has to land before the cheaper detector does.

field.thesis: A detection pipeline that cannot be observed has three compounding defects — invisible, expensive, unmeasurable — and the fix order runs observability first, because capability without observability only adds another invisible writer.

sections.title: Invisible, expensive, unmeasurable
sections.claim: The three defects compound, and unmeasurability is what locks the other two in place.
sections.receipt: 181 jobs died with the same HTTP failure code across all five retries — the signature of a shared-egress rate limit amplified by a queue with no backoff.

sections.title: The fix is ordered
sections.claim: Build the surface before the detector; the surface is what makes the detector landable.
sections.receipt: Geometry is already stored as normalized polygons in [0,1], so the page overlay needs no coordinate math — the data was ready to be seen the whole time.

sections.title: The free detector
sections.claim: The cheap detector already exists in pieces; the work is generalizing the split into a recursive XY-cut.
sections.receipt: Transparent margins naively flattened to RGB render black and fabricate the exact dark bands a gutter detector keys on.

sections.title: Ground truth, in order of cost
sections.claim: Score the detector on a ladder ordered by cost and by what each rung can honestly claim.
sections.receipt: Cross-engine agreement is free and covers real pages, but two detectors sharing a blind spot agree perfectly — so report the disagreements rather than averaging them away.

sections.title: The bug I shipped while planning this
sections.claim: A system you cannot see does not only hide its own failures; it launders yours.
sections.receipt: Code classified ground truth on state `confirmed`, an enum value that does not exist — the schema is candidate | accepted | verified | rejected — so the UI rendered 'No region has been confirmed' as a fact.

relatedArticles.reason: Both argue that a system's account of itself is infrastructure, not commentary — documentation and detection surfaces fail the same way when nothing reads them.
The measurement discipline this piece applies to a detector, stated formally: what a claim may honestly assert given the evidence behind it.
Inferring an enum from surrounding prose instead of reading the schema is the failure this piece warns about, met in production.

seo.title: Why Interaction Became a Scientific Problem
seo.description: Four decades of human-computer interaction, from Bush and Engelbart to Suchman, Hutchins, and Dourish, and the question the field kept postponing: what, exactly, is an interaction? Why AI forces it, and why it needs a science, not another methodology.

frontmatter.coverAlt: A painted technical drawing on textured off-white paper. On the left, a dense lattice of ruled lines, circles, and hatching in ink and blue wash, standing for a system's internal state. A firm vertical line marks a boundary. To its right a single horizontal path continues as a dotted line that branches into several forks before trailing off, standing for what a person observes and infers from the system.
frontmatter.caption: System and projection. The dense structure at left is what a computational system is; the sparse, forking trace at right is what a person observes and infers. The essay is about the gap between them.
frontmatter.authorNote: The first in a series introducing Foundations of Computational Interaction. This one earns the question; it does not yet answer it.
